title: When Are Kids Old Enough for R-Rated Movies?

content: Illustration by Dale Stephanos My teenage son, Milo, doesn’t love seeing scary stuff, like Stephen King trailers, eerie clowns, or Stranger Things . I can’t blame him. I’ve never paid money to be frightened. But he wanted to give Stranger Things another shot with a friend who was into the show. The plan was to watch at the friend’s house on a Saturday afternoon, but on Saturday morning, the other dad wasn’t feeling well, and we don’t have the space or second television to handle a day-long marathon. They ended up going to my sister-in-law’s, a great pivot, complete with a third-floor television room and a mini fridge filled with Cokes. When Milo got home, we found out that one episode was enough for him. They instead had their own Plan B. They watched Stripes . Since my wife has never been a 13-year-old boy in 1981, the ensuing thought pattern never came into her head. Good choice. One of the funniest movies ever. He saw boobs. For some context, it’s nothing graphic or objectifying, says the man who was 13 years old in 1981. The visuals are fairly tame, and the mud-wrestling scene is key to the dramatic arc. Still, it’s bare boobs, and the kids are 14. I have no problem if my child sees them. It’s the offering it up to someone else’s child that made me think that this day wasn’t going on the highlight reel. A heads-up text probably should have been sent. No, it definitely should have been sent. Without question. Should have been sent. What would I have written? Ahhhhhhh… Kids want to watch Stripes . You good? Nope. Just a heads-up. Kids are… Nope. Hey, how’s this for problem-solving? Nope. In the big picture, I don’t think this was the worst parenting mistake ever, but I also don’t think I’m in the position to judge the lingering effects. Then I started reviewing my own childhood, one filled with Cinemax in a first-floor den out of earshot of my parents’ second-floor bedroom. I also remember my friend John Fields’s sleepover birthday, during which we watched Animal House . It’s another one of the funniest movies ever, and it also gave us the chance to see boobs more than once, particularly since we watched it three times that night. Oh, and we were in fifth grade. This was the 1970s, not the apex of hands-on parenting. My mom and dad cared about me, but not so much in a probing way. They certainly didn’t care about what I was watching after dark. My mother only learned about Animal House six sentences ago. But they also weren’t absentee, and they couldn’t always claim plausible deniability to what I was watching. When I was in sixth grade, they took me to see 10 . An eyeful, I’ll say, and while captivated, I questioned whether I should really be seeing this with my parents. My mom’s reasoning afterward was that she didn’t realize what an R rating was. I think she’d like to have that one back, although no apology has ever been needed. Two years later, it was Richard Pryor: Live on the Sunset Strip , which, upon review, was kind of badass, as though my parents were saying, “No, Journey will not be your first concert. We’re seeing the Ramones.” My only regret, and I knew this as it was happening, was that I sat in front of them and couldn’t see what they were laughing at. I’m not sure if Pryor was the same kind of whiff. The language was hard, and he was talking about setting himself on fire. But I was 13. I knew a lot of the words already, and possibly my parents thought I could handle it. Or maybe they didn’t realize how Pryor actually talked. Or maybe they wanted to see it, and so they brought me along, banking on the fact that I didn’t always emulate everything I watched. I loved Raiders of the Lost Ark . Never once asked to take an archaeology class. Rocky , excellent. Getting hit, not at all. And as for 10 ? It never made me say, “I gotta go run, and it’s gotta be on a beach.” But now, I’m in the hot seat. Milo is almost 15, his brother, Levi, almost 12. Their movie tastes are changing, and they’re asking when they can see The Godfather , a totally reasonable and admirable question for which I have no answer. I wish there were a simple equation or app that would tell the right time, but… “There’s no fixed rule. There’s no speed limit,” says Gene Beresin, executive director of the Clay Center for Healthy Young Minds at Massachusetts General Hospital and professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School. “As parents, we all have to make judgments.” Eff. Eff. Eff. Eff. Eff. I was afraid of this. I want to not care like my parents did. I want to be more whatever. I don’t want to have to decide, but this is yet another reminder that I’m the adult in charge, and I know when it’s the best time for them to see a movie about loyalty, secrets, deception, seduction, and a guy getting shot in the eye while getting a massage. But I’m worried. What if I screw up, and it wasn’t the right time? Then it wasn’t the right time. It’s called making a mistake. It’s what parents do. It’s what I do fairly regularly. I yell. I’m quick to judge. I withdraw for foolish reasons. I forget to bring the water bottle that was sitting on the stairs and that I was reminded to bring. When Levi was eight, I bought him Flamin’ Hot Cheetos for a snack, because somehow, I didn’t fully understand what flaming hot meant. He constantly reminds me of this, often when he’s about to get a snack. I wonder, though, if I should have been there to watch Stripes with Milo in order to help him process what he saw. God no. Stripes is not a movie that you see with your dad. That’s Casablanca or Die Hard . Milo needed to take it all in and make sense of it on his own and laugh without wondering what I was laughing at. He needed to handle the unexpected and walk away if he must, just like he did with Stranger Things . But I can be there some of the time. I took Levi to see Young Frankenstein in June. Scary but not scary good film. Everything was going well, and Oh, there’s the implied sex scene in the hay between the awesome Madeline Kahn and Peter Boyle’s monster . Maybe I should check in with him, just so he’s not wondering or worried that that’s what happens in hay or with monsters. Did I? No. It might have gone right past him; I’m hoping for that at least, because I know that happens. My parents took me to a lot of grown-up films, and I came out with my own takeaways. M*A*S*H . (The shower tent fell down.) The Sting . (Paul Newman burped.) Blazing Saddles . (Sorry, horse.) We’re good worriers, my wife and I, but we brought the kids to the original The Bad News Bears when it was playing on the big screen at the Brattle this spring. They were both in their baseball seasons, so the timing seemed perfect. It was all going well, and then, Oh, I forgot about Tanner’s rant where he says almost every slur against every person who’s not him . I thought the film was a success, but you don’t know unless you ask. And so I asked how they liked the movie. They loved the movie. I asked their favorite part, and the answer was unanimous. “When the kid kicked him in the balls.” I couldn’t argue. It was a well-delivered and understandable rebuke to enduring a season of constant disrespect and marginalization. When we were walking out, Levi added, “Movies were just so much better back then.” I kind of think he’s picking up on the more relaxed pace or seeing a time that looked riskier and more fun—bikes without helmets, big convertibles, and kids sitting up on the back of moving big convertibles. Afterward, at lunch, we made a list of all the things in the movie that would never be in a movie today. No personal equipment bags. Eating hot dogs right after a game without wiping your hands. A coach smoking around kids. A coach drinking around kids. A coach passing out at practice. A coach handing out beers to his players. Those players pouring the beer on each other . We stopped at 30. As a youth baseball coach, I am not advocating for, nor will I be looking to bring back, any of the above. But I enjoyed watching what we once were. I want to be able to do it more often. I want more chances to see old movies on the big screen. The sound is better, and no one is finding a reason to go into the kitchen to see what’s in the fridge. Some theaters already program old flicks, but not enough. Reboots are all the rage in Hollywood. This is the ultimate, original reboot. I don’t see the downside of showing The Princess Bride once a month. Yeah, yeah. Variety. Yeah, yeah. Point of diminishing returns. Don’t care. Some people might complain. Don’t care. I want Ghostbusters , Bull Durham , and all the other movies I want at times that are good for me and my family. I want some well-placed f-bombs, Indiana bike races, raw egg yolks, flux capacitors, more Karen Allen, and some tasteful, random, quick-before-you-miss-them boob shots. It’s not for me. It’s for my kids. It’s for the kids. If they miss out, well, that would be the worst kick in the nuts.
